design-safety-001.question: Which correctly describes the difference between a process flow diagram (PFD) and a piping and instrumentation diagram (P&ID)?
choices: The PFD shows all piping, valves and instruments, while the P&ID shows only the major equipment
The PFD shows the major equipment, the main flows and the mass and heat balances (flow rates, temperatures, pressures), while the P&ID shows piping, valves, instruments and control loops in detail
PFD and P&ID are two names for the same drawing
design-safety-001.explanation: The PFD shows the skeleton of the process: the major equipment and main flows, the number of each stream and its mass and heat balance data such as flow rate, composition, temperature and pressure, and the main control philosophy. The P&ID is the basis for detailed design, operation and maintenance, and shows all piping (size, material, line number), manual valves, control valves and safety valves, instruments and control loops, interlocks, and even drains and vents. The choice in which the PFD shows every pipe, valve and instrument has the amount of detail backwards. The two are separate drawings with different purposes. Safety reviews such as HAZOP are usually carried out on the P&ID.

design-safety-002.question: What does an instrument labeled “TIC” on a P&ID mean (ISA instrument symbols)?
choices: An instrument that indicates and controls temperature (temperature indicating controller)
An instrument that totalizes flow
An interlock that shuts down equipment when the temperature becomes abnormal
design-safety-002.explanation: In ISA instrument symbols, the first letter is the measured variable and the following letters are functions. T is temperature, I is indicator and C is controller, so TIC is a temperature indicating controller. Similarly, FIC is a flow indicating controller, LT a level transmitter and PSV a pressure safety valve. Flow totalizing is shown by a different symbol, FQ (Q for totalize), and a switch that acts on high temperature by TSH, for example. Being able to read the symbols lets you work out the structure of the control loops from a P&ID.

design-safety-003.question: How is the control valve on the cooling water to the jacket of an exothermic reactor generally chosen to behave when instrument air or the signal is lost?
choices: It goes fully closed (fail closed, air-to-open)
It holds its current opening (fail last)
It goes fully open (fail open, air-to-close)
design-safety-003.explanation: When instrument air or the signal is lost, a pneumatic control valve moves to a fixed position under spring force, so the valve type is chosen according to which direction is safe. If the cooling water to an exothermic reactor stops, the temperature rises and can lead to a runaway reaction, so the cooling-water valve is generally chosen to fail open (air-to-close). Conversely, supply valves for fuel gas or reactor feed are chosen to fail closed (air-to-open). Valves that hold their position also exist, but their position is not guaranteed over time, so types that move reliably to the safe side are preferred.

design-safety-004.question: Approximately what inside diameter of circular pipe is needed to carry water at a volumetric flow rate of 0.020 m³/s at a mean velocity of 2.0 m/s?
choices: About 56 mm
100 mm
About 113 mm
design-safety-004.explanation: The required cross-sectional area is A = Q/u = 0.020 ÷ 2.0 = 0.010 m². From the area of a circle A = πD²/4, D = √(4A/π) = √0.0127 ≈ 0.113 m, or about 113 mm. 100 mm treats the cross section as a square with side √A, and about 56 mm mistakes the radius, √(A/π), for the diameter. Pipe sizes are chosen around velocities of roughly 1–3 m/s for liquids and 10–30 m/s for gases, balancing pressure drop and pump power against piping cost. In practice a standard pipe size is selected and the resulting velocity and pressure drop are checked.

design-safety-005.question: A stirred tank is scaled up with geometric similarity, doubling every dimension. By what factor does the jacket heat transfer area per unit volume of reaction liquid change?
choices: 2 times
1/2 times
It does not change
design-safety-005.explanation: Doubling the dimensions makes areas 2² = 4 times and volumes 2³ = 8 times larger, so the heat transfer area per unit volume becomes 4/8 = 1/2. In an exothermic reaction the heat generated grows in proportion to volume, while the heat that can be removed grows only in proportion to area, so heat removal that was no problem in small equipment can fall behind when it is scaled up. This is one reason temperature runaways are more likely on scale-up, and it is dealt with by adding internal coils or an external circulation heat exchanger, or by adding feed gradually (semibatch operation). Answering 2 times or no change overlooks the difference in how area and volume grow.

design-safety-006.question: Which correctly describes how a HAZOP (hazard and operability study) is carried out?
choices: For each section of the P&ID (node), guidewords are combined with parameters such as flow, temperature and pressure to postulate deviations from the design intent, and their causes, consequences and safeguards are examined
An undesired top event is defined, its causes are broken down into a tree with AND and OR gates, and its probability of occurrence is calculated
Failure modes are listed for each piece of equipment or component, and the effect of each on the system is summarized in a table
design-safety-006.explanation: HAZOP is a qualitative method for systematically identifying deviations from the design intent. A multidisciplinary team from operations, design, instrumentation, safety and other fields works through each node, combining guidewords (no, more, less, reverse and so on) with parameters (for example, no flow, high temperature, reverse flow). For each deviation, the causes, consequences, existing safeguards and additional recommendations are recorded. Breaking a top event down into causes and calculating its probability is fault tree analysis (FTA), and summarizing the effects of each failure mode is failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA); these take a different viewpoint.

design-safety-007.question: In a HAZOP, which deviation is most appropriate to postulate when the guideword “reverse” is combined with the parameter “flow”?
choices: The pump stops and there is no flow in the line
The pressure in the downstream reactor exceeds the pump discharge pressure, and reaction liquid flows back toward the feed tank
The control valve opens too far and the flow exceeds the design value
design-safety-007.explanation: “Reverse” is the guideword for flow in the opposite direction to that intended. If the downstream pressure becomes higher than upstream, reaction liquid flows back into the feed tank, which can cause unexpected reactions, contamination or overpressure in the feed tank. Safeguards to consider include check valves, shutoff valves with interlocks, and pressure monitoring. Loss of flow when the pump stops is the deviation postulated with “no”, and too much flow is the one postulated with “more”. Applying the guidewords in turn reduces omissions without relying on whatever comes to mind.

design-safety-008.question: Which is the correct approach to the set pressure (opening pressure) of a safety valve fitted to a pressure vessel?
choices: Set it at or below the vessel's design pressure (maximum allowable working pressure), with a margin above the normal operating pressure
Set it below the normal operating pressure and keep it relieving slightly at all times during operation
Set it at about twice the vessel's design pressure
design-safety-008.explanation: A safety valve is the last line of protection, relieving excess fluid to keep the vessel pressure from exceeding its design limit. Its set pressure is therefore at or below the vessel's design pressure (maximum allowable working pressure), and its size is chosen from the required relief rate so that the pressure rise while relieving stays within what codes allow. Setting it below the operating pressure means it relieves constantly, losing contents and damaging the valve seat. So that the valve does not leak or lift during operation, a common guideline is to keep the operating pressure at or below about 90% of the set pressure (this depends on the valve type). A setting of twice the design pressure would not protect the vessel.

design-safety-009.question: Which correctly describes a rupture disk?
choices: After opening at its set pressure, it closes automatically when the pressure falls and can be used again
It acts more slowly than a safety valve, so it is unsuitable for rapid pressure rises
Once it acts it does not reclose and must be replaced, but it is simple, leak-free and suited to corrosive fluids and rapid pressure rises
design-safety-009.explanation: A rupture disk opens a flow path when a thin metal disk or similar element bursts at a specified pressure. With no moving parts it acts quickly, and it does not leak in normal service. This makes it suitable for corrosive or fouling fluids and for protection against rapid pressure rises such as runaway reactions. On the other hand, once it bursts it does not reclose, so the contents keep escaping and it must be replaced. Reclosing when the pressure falls is a feature of spring-loaded safety valves. A rupture disk is also sometimes installed at the inlet of a safety valve to protect the valve from corrosive fluids.

design-safety-010.question: Which is closest to the flammable (explosive) range of methane in air at room temperature and atmospheric pressure?
choices: About 4–75 vol%
About 5–15 vol%
About 1.4–7.6 vol%
design-safety-010.explanation: The lower flammable limit of methane is about 5 vol% and the upper limit about 15 vol%; a flame propagates through a mixture in this range if there is an ignition source. About 4–75 vol% is the range for hydrogen, which needs particular care because its range is wide and its ignition energy small. About 1.4–7.6 vol% is roughly the range for gasoline vapor; the lower a flammable substance's lower limit, the more easily a small leak reaches a dangerous concentration. The flammable range widens as temperature rises, and in oxygen the upper limit widens greatly. Keeping well below the lower limit (ventilation and dilution) or lowering the oxygen concentration with inert gas is the basis of explosion prevention.

design-safety-011.question: Using Le Chatelier's rule 1/L = Σ(yᵢ/Lᵢ), approximately what is the lower flammable limit in air of a fuel gas consisting of 50 vol% methane and 50 vol% propane? Take the lower flammable limit of methane as 5.0 vol% and of propane as 2.1 vol% (yᵢ is the mole fraction of each component in the fuel gas).
choices: About 3.0 vol%
About 3.6 vol%
2.1 vol%
design-safety-011.explanation: 1/L = 0.50/5.0 + 0.50/2.1 = 0.100 + 0.238 = 0.338, so L ≈ 1/0.338 ≈ 3.0 vol%. The lower limit of a mixture is strongly influenced by the component with the lower limit, and is lower than the simple arithmetic mean of about 3.6 vol% ((5.0 + 2.1)/2). 2.1 vol% is the value for propane alone; because the mixture contains methane, its lower limit is higher. Le Chatelier's rule fits mixtures of similar hydrocarbons relatively well, but errors can be large when components with very different properties, such as hydrogen, are present.

design-safety-012.question: A vessel full of air at atmospheric pressure (21 vol% O2) is pressurized with nitrogen to 500 kPa absolute, mixed, and then vented to atmospheric pressure (taken as 100 kPa). This is repeated twice. Approximately what is the oxygen concentration in the vessel (constant temperature, complete mixing)?
choices: 4.2 vol%
About 2.1 vol%
About 0.84 vol%
design-safety-012.explanation: Pressurizing from 100 kPa to 500 kPa absolute with nitrogen leaves the amount of oxygen unchanged while multiplying the total moles by five, so the oxygen concentration falls to 21 × (100/500) = 4.2 vol%. Venting to atmospheric pressure does not change the concentration, and the second pressurization cuts it by another factor of five, to 4.2 × 0.2 = 0.84 vol%. 4.2 vol% is the value after just one cycle, and about 2.1 vol% is the mistake of adding the dilution factors (5 + 5 = 10 times) instead of multiplying them. After n cycles the concentration is multiplied by (low pressure/high pressure) to the nth power. Nitrogen purging before flammable gas is introduced reduces the oxygen concentration to the target in this way.

design-safety-013.question: Which is the generally recommended relationship between a safety instrumented system (SIS, interlocks such as emergency shutdown) and the basic process control system (BPCS) used for normal operation?
choices: They share the same controllers and sensors and serve both roles with different set points
The safety instrumented system is built from sensors, logic solvers and final elements independent of the basic control system, so that a failure in one does not spread to the other
As long as there is a basic control system, safety instrumentation is unnecessary
design-safety-013.explanation: In the protection-layer concept, basic control, alarms with operator response, safety instrumentation, mechanical protection such as safety valves, and mitigation such as dikes each act as independent layers that stop an incident from escalating. A failure of a basic-control sensor or controller can itself be the cause of an abnormal situation, so if the same equipment is shared, the cause and the protection are lost at the same time. Safety instrumentation is therefore built from independent sensors, logic solvers and shutoff valves, and designed and tested according to the required reliability (SIL). Relying on basic control alone means having only one protection layer.

design-safety-014.question: In the economic evaluation of a capital investment, which is correct about depreciation?
choices: It allocates the cost of acquiring the equipment as an expense over its useful life, and the same amount of cash does not actually leave that year
Each year, cash equal to the acquisition cost of the equipment is paid out
The larger the depreciation, the higher the taxable income and the more tax is paid
design-safety-014.explanation: Depreciation is the mechanism for spreading the acquisition cost of equipment used for many years as an expense over its period of use. With the straight-line method, the annual amount is (acquisition cost − salvage value) ÷ useful life; for example, ¥12 million of equipment with a salvage value of ¥2 million depreciated over 10 years gives ¥1 million per year. The actual cash leaves at the time of purchase, so depreciation is a noncash expense, and cash flow is found as after-tax profit + depreciation. Because depreciation is an expense that reduces taxable income, it works to reduce taxes.

design-safety-015.question: Installing ¥30 million of energy-saving equipment cuts annual energy costs by ¥8 million but raises maintenance costs by ¥2 million per year. Ignoring taxes and the time value of money, approximately what is the simple payback period?
choices: 3.0 years
3.75 years
5.0 years
design-safety-015.explanation: The simple payback period is the investment ÷ the net annual savings. The net savings are 8 − 2 = ¥6 million per year, so 30 ÷ 6 = 5.0 years. 3.75 years ignores the increase in maintenance costs and calculates 30 ÷ 8, and 3.0 years adds the maintenance cost to the savings (30 ÷ 10). The simple payback period is easy to understand, but it ignores profits after payback and the time value of money, so for large investment decisions it is used together with net present value (NPV) and the internal rate of return (IRR).
